title: The Journey of a Packet
summary: When you send a photo, it is chopped into thousands of tiny numbered pieces called packets. Each one races through cables and routers, maybe by a different road, and the computer at the other end clicks them back together like a jigsaw. If a piece goes missing, it simply asks for it again!

sections.heading: One Tap, Two Thousand Travellers
paragraphs: Imagine you have just taken a funny photo of your dog wearing sunglasses, and you want to send it to your cousin who lives on the other side of an ocean. You tap Send. Less than a second later, your cousin's phone buzzes. It feels like magic, as if the picture simply jumped from one screen to the other.

It did not jump. In that blink of an eye, your photo was cut into roughly two thousand small pieces. Each piece was wrapped in a label, handed to your Wi-Fi router, pushed into a copper wire or a glass fibre, passed from one machine to the next across a country, shot under the sea as flashes of light, and handed along again until it reached your cousin's phone. There, every piece was checked, counted and snapped back into place in exactly the right order. If even one piece got lost on the way, your cousin's phone noticed and asked for it again.

In Part 6 we met Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn and their rules called TCP/IP, which let many different networks join into one Internet. Rules on paper are one thing, though. In this part we are going to follow those rules in action. We will shrink ourselves down to the size of a single packet and ride along on its journey, the way you might follow one letter through a giant postal system.

Along the way you will learn what data really is, what a packet looks like inside, what routers do all day, why packets sometimes arrive in a jumble, and how TCP, the careful bookkeeper of the Internet, makes sure nothing is missing. By the end, you will be able to read the kind of list network engineers use to watch a packet hop across the world, with times measured in thousandths of a second.

One important idea before we set off: nobody steers your packet from start to finish. There is no central control room watching it. Each machine along the way makes one small decision, passes the packet on, and forgets about it. The whole amazing journey is built out of thousands of these tiny, local decisions. That is exactly what the packet-switching pioneers of Part 3 had in mind.

sections.heading: Everything Is Ones and Zeros
paragraphs: Before we can understand packets, we need to understand what is inside them. Computers do not store pictures, songs or words the way we see and hear them. They store everything as numbers, and those numbers are written using only two digits: 1 and 0. Each single 1 or 0 is called a bit, short for 'binary digit'. Eight bits grouped together make a byte.

Why only two digits? Because two states are easy to make and hard to confuse. A wire can have a voltage or not. A tiny spot on a chip can hold an electric charge or not. A laser in a fibre-optic cable can flash or stay dark. A radio wave can shift one way or another. Telling 'on' from 'off' is much more reliable than telling apart ten different levels, especially when a signal has travelled thousands of kilometres and become faint and noisy.

So how does a letter become bits? Computers use agreed codes. In the common ASCII code, which dates back to the 1960s, the capital letter A is the number 65. Written in binary, 65 is 01000001, which fits neatly into one byte. Lower-case a is 97, and the digit 7 is 55. Modern text uses a bigger code called Unicode, which can also store Chinese characters, Arabic letters and even emoji, sometimes using two, three or four bytes for one symbol.

Pictures are made of pixels, tiny coloured squares. In a typical colour image, each pixel is stored as three numbers: how much red, how much green and how much blue it contains, each from 0 to 255. That is three bytes per pixel. A 12-megapixel phone photo has about 12 million pixels, which would be about 36 million bytes if stored plainly. Clever compression, like the JPEG format, squeezes this down, often to just a few million bytes, by throwing away details your eyes would hardly notice.

Sound works in a similar way. A microphone turns air vibrations into a wobbling electrical signal, and the computer measures that signal thousands of times every second. Music on a CD, for example, was measured 44,100 times per second for each of the two stereo channels. Every measurement becomes a number, and every number becomes bits.

This is the secret that makes the Internet possible. Because text, photos, voices, videos and game moves all become the same thing, long strings of 1s and 0s, one single network can carry all of them. The network does not need to know whether it is carrying a birthday message or a dinosaur documentary. It just carries bits.

sections.heading: Inside a Packet: Label and Load
paragraphs: Now imagine your dog photo as a long ribbon of about three million bytes. The Internet will not send that whole ribbon in one go. Instead, it chops it into packets. On Ethernet cables and most home networks, the largest packet allowed is about 1,500 bytes. Engineers call this limit the MTU, short for maximum transmission unit. So a 3-megabyte photo needs roughly two thousand packets.

Every packet has two main parts. The first part is the header, which is like the address label and stamp on an envelope. The second part is the payload, which is the actual slice of data being carried, a small strip of your photo. A good way to picture it is a long letter cut up into numbered postcards. Each postcard carries a few lines of the letter on one side and the address and its number on the other.

What is written in the header? For the classic version of the Internet Protocol, IPv4, described in a document called RFC 791 in September 1981, the header is usually 20 bytes long. It contains the address of the computer that sent the packet and the address of the computer it is going to. Each address is 32 bits long. It also says which version of IP is being used, how long the whole packet is, and which kind of message is inside, for example a TCP message.

One clever field is called time to live, or TTL. It is a small number, up to 255, and every router that handles the packet lowers it by one. If it ever reaches zero, the packet is thrown away. Why build in a self-destruct counter? Because if something goes wrong and routers accidentally pass a packet round in a circle, it would otherwise go round forever, clogging the network. With TTL, a lost packet eventually just fades away.

There is also a checksum, a number calculated from the header's contents. Each router recalculates it. If the numbers do not match, the header has been damaged on the way, perhaps by electrical noise, and the packet is discarded rather than being sent somewhere wrong.

Inside the IP packet sits a second header, the TCP header, which is usually another 20 bytes. It holds a sequence number, which tells the receiver where this slice belongs in the whole message, and an acknowledgement number, used to tell the other side what has arrived safely. So of the 1,500 bytes in a full packet, about 40 bytes are labels and about 1,460 are your photo. Only around 3 percent of the space goes on paperwork, which is a pretty good deal.

sections.heading: Envelopes Inside Envelopes
paragraphs: Engineers have a favourite trick for keeping a complicated system understandable: they split it into layers. Each layer has one job and only needs to talk to the layers just above and below it. The Internet is usually described with four or five layers, and the easiest way to imagine them is as envelopes tucked inside other envelopes.

At the top is the application layer. This is the program you are using, such as a messaging app, a web browser or a game. It decides what to say, for example 'here is a photo for my cousin'. Web browsers use a set of rules called HTTP at this layer, which you will meet properly in later parts of this story.

Next comes the transport layer, where TCP lives. TCP takes the app's data, cuts it into pieces of the right size, and puts each piece into its own envelope with a sequence number. It also adds a port number, a bit like a flat number in a big apartment building, so that the right program on the receiving computer gets the data. Your phone might be running a video, a chat app and a weather widget all at once, and port numbers keep their packets from getting mixed up.

Then comes the Internet layer, where IP lives. IP puts the TCP envelope inside a bigger envelope marked with the source and destination IP addresses. This is the envelope that routers read when deciding where to send things.

Below that is the link layer, which handles one single step of the journey: from your laptop to your Wi-Fi router, say, or from one router to the next along a fibre. Wi-Fi and Ethernet each wrap the IP packet in their own outer envelope, with local hardware addresses that only matter for that one hop. Finally, at the very bottom, is the physical layer: the actual radio waves, electrical pulses or flashes of light that carry the bits.

Here is the beautiful part. When a router receives a packet, it opens only the outer, link-layer envelope. It reads the IP envelope's destination, decides the next step, and then wraps the packet in a fresh outer envelope for the next link. It does not need to open the TCP envelope, and it certainly does not look at your photo. The packet might travel by Wi-Fi, then copper, then fibre under the sea, then radio again, changing its outer envelope at every step, while the inner envelopes ride along unchanged.

Layers also mean that inventors can improve one layer without breaking the others. When Wi-Fi got faster, nobody had to rewrite email. When new apps were invented, nobody had to rebuild the cables. Engineers sometimes draw this as an hourglass: lots of different apps at the top, lots of different cables and radios at the bottom, and one slim waist in the middle where everything passes through IP. That narrow, shared middle is a big reason the Internet has been able to grow and change for decades.

sections.heading: Routers: The Sorting Offices of the Internet
paragraphs: Picture a giant postal sorting office at night. Letters pour in on conveyor belts. A worker glances at each address, does not read the letter, and drops it into the bin for the right next van: this one to the north, this one to the airport, this one to the town down the road. The worker does not know the whole route the letter will take. They only know which van gets it one step closer.

A router does exactly this, but with packets, and unimaginably fast. A router is a specialised computer with several connections, called interfaces. When a packet arrives on one interface, the router reads the destination IP address in its header, looks it up in a list called a routing table, and sends the packet out of whichever interface leads one step closer. Each step from one router to the next is called a hop.

A routing table does not list every computer in the world. That would be impossible. Instead, it lists groups of addresses that share the same beginning, a bit like a sorting office knowing that every postcode starting with a certain letter goes to the same region. Most home routers have a very short table that basically says: 'If it is for a device in this house, send it here; for everything else, send it to the Internet provider.' That catch-all instruction is called the default route.

Big routers deep inside the Internet, owned by phone companies and network providers, have enormous tables with hundreds of thousands of entries. These machines can sit in tall metal racks in buildings full of humming equipment, and the largest of them can forward huge numbers of packets every second. To keep their tables up to date, routers constantly chat with their neighbours using routing protocols, sharing news such as 'I can reach these addresses' or 'that link has just broken'. If a cable is cut, routers learn about it and start sending packets around the damaged area, often within seconds or minutes.

How many hops does a packet usually take? It depends on where it is going, but a typical trip across the Internet often passes through somewhere around 10 to 20 routers. A message to a website in your own city might need fewer; one going to the other side of the planet might need more.

Routers do not have unlimited room. Each one keeps a small waiting area for packets, called a buffer or queue, like a line at a ticket window. When too many packets arrive at once, the queue grows, and packets wait a little longer. If the queue completely fills up, the router has no choice but to drop new packets on the floor. This sounds alarming, but the Internet was designed expecting it. IP itself makes no promises. It does its best to deliver each packet, but if one is lost, it is someone else's job to notice. That someone is TCP.

sections.heading: Different Roads, Jumbled Arrivals
paragraphs: Because every router makes its own decision for each packet, two packets from the same photo do not have to travel the same way. Most of the time they do follow the same path, because routers tend to keep sending traffic for one destination down the same route. But routes can change in the middle of a conversation. A link may get busy, a cable may be repaired and switched back on, or a router may spread traffic over two equally good paths to share the load.

This means packets can arrive out of order. Packet number 5 might arrive before packet number 4, just as a postcard sent on Tuesday sometimes beats one sent on Monday. Some might be delayed by a long queue. One might be dropped by a busy router. Very occasionally, one might even be delivered twice.

To a telephone engineer of the 1960s, this would have sounded like chaos. In a phone call, as we saw in Part 1, a whole circuit is reserved for you, and your voice flows along it in perfect order. But that reserved line sits idle whenever you pause for breath. Packet switching gives up that perfect, private road in exchange for something much more efficient: many conversations sharing the same lines at the same time, with each line kept busy almost all the time.

Louis Pouzin's idea of the datagram, which we met in Part 6, is at work here. Each IP packet is a datagram: a self-contained message that carries its full destination address and can find its own way, without the network remembering anything about the conversation it belongs to. The network in the middle stays simple and fast. All the hard work of making things neat and complete is pushed out to the two computers at the edges. That is the 'end-to-end' principle, and it is one of the Internet's deepest design ideas.
So the question becomes: how do the computers at the edges turn a messy shower of packets, some late, some missing, some swapped around, back into a perfect photo of a dog in sunglasses?

sections.heading: TCP: The Careful Bookkeeper
paragraphs: TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol, is the part of the Internet that takes unreliable packet delivery and turns it into a reliable stream of data. Its rules were written down in RFC 793, published in September 1981, and they have been improved many times since. You can think of TCP as a very patient bookkeeper sitting at each end of the conversation.

First, TCP says hello. Before any data is sent, the two computers perform a three-way handshake. Your phone sends a packet marked SYN, short for synchronise, which means roughly 'I would like to talk, and I will start counting from this number.' The other computer replies with SYN-ACK: 'Got it, and here is my starting number too.' Your phone answers ACK: 'Great, got yours.' Now both sides know the other is listening and have agreed on how to count.

Second, TCP numbers everything. Its sequence numbers actually count bytes, not packets, so each packet's header says something like 'this piece starts at byte 14,601 of the message.' When pieces arrive out of order, the receiver puts them in their correct place, like slotting numbered jigsaw pieces into the right gaps. If a piece arrives twice, it simply ignores the copy.

Third, TCP says thank you. The receiver regularly sends back acknowledgements, often shortened to ACKs. An acknowledgement says, 'I have everything up to byte such-and-such, and I am now waiting for the next one.' The sender keeps a copy of every piece it has sent until it is acknowledged.

Fourth, TCP tries again. When the sender sends a packet, it starts a timer. If no acknowledgement arrives before the timer runs out, TCP assumes the packet was lost and sends it again. TCP also learns how long round trips usually take, so it does not wait too long or give up too quickly. Modern TCP has extra tricks too: if the receiver keeps acknowledging the same point again and again, the sender can guess that one piece is missing and resend it straight away, without waiting for the timer.

Fifth, TCP checks for damage. Every TCP piece carries a checksum covering its data. If a single bit has been flipped by noise, the numbers will not add up, and the receiver throws the piece away so it will be sent again.

Finally, TCP is polite. Each acknowledgement tells the sender how much more room the receiver has, so a fast computer does not drown a slow one. TCP also watches for signs of traffic jams. In October 1986, the early Internet suffered what engineers called a congestion collapse: on one link between Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory and the University of California, Berkeley, useful data slowed from about 32,000 bits per second to about 40, because computers kept resending lost packets into an already overloaded network. The researcher Van Jacobson and his colleague Michael Karels worked out rules, published in 1988, that make TCP slow down when packets are being lost and speed up gently when things are clear. Those ideas, refined over the years, still help keep the Internet from jamming today.

Not every app wants all this care. For a live video call or a fast online game, a packet that arrives late is useless anyway, because the moment has already passed. Those apps often use a simpler partner protocol called UDP, which sends packets with no handshake, no numbering checks and no resending. A tiny glitch in a video call is better than the whole call freezing while TCP waits for one missing piece.

sections.heading: Watching a Packet Cross the Ocean
paragraphs: Can we actually see a packet's journey? Almost. In 1987, the network researcher Van Jacobson wrote a small program called traceroute, building on a suggestion from Steve Deering. It is still used by network engineers today, and many computers have a version of it built in (on Windows it is called tracert).

Traceroute uses a sneaky trick with the time-to-live counter. It sends a packet with a TTL of just 1. The very first router lowers it to zero, throws the packet away, and politely sends back a short error message saying 'time exceeded', which reveals that router's address. Then traceroute sends a packet with a TTL of 2, which dies at the second router, and so on, one hop further each time, until a packet finally reaches the destination. By timing each reply, traceroute shows how long the round trip to each router takes, usually trying three times per hop. If a router does not answer, traceroute prints a star instead.

Let us imagine a traceroute from a home in London to a website server in New York. The exact names and numbers would be different for every real connection, so treat this as a typical example rather than a real record. Hop 1 is your home Wi-Fi router, reached in about 2 milliseconds, that is, two thousandths of a second. Hops 2 to 4 are routers belonging to your Internet provider in your town and in central London, at about 5 to 10 milliseconds. Hop 5 might be a big exchange building where many networks meet. Then comes the big jump: at hop 6 or 7, the time suddenly leaps from about 10 milliseconds to around 70 or 75. That leap is the Atlantic Ocean. The last few hops, inside New York, add only a millisecond or two each, and the server answers at hop 12 or so.

Why is crossing the ocean so slow, when light is the fastest thing there is? Light in empty space travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second. But inside a glass fibre it slows to about 200,000 kilometres per second, roughly two-thirds of its full speed, because glass bends and slows light. London and New York are about 5,600 kilometres apart in a straight line, and real cables follow longer paths across the seabed and over land. At 200,000 kilometres per second, every 200 kilometres of fibre adds about one millisecond. So a cable path of about 6,000 kilometres takes roughly 30 milliseconds one way, and about 60 there and back. Add a few milliseconds for routers, queues and detours, and you get the 70-odd milliseconds that traceroute shows. The delay is mostly just the speed of light.

Seventy milliseconds is less than the time it takes you to blink, which is usually about a tenth of a second or more. So all two thousand pieces of your dog photo can make the journey, be checked, reordered and acknowledged, and appear on your cousin's screen in well under a second. Packet by packet, hop by hop, the Internet quietly does its job.

But wait. Every router along the way had to read a destination address, a long string of numbers, to know where to send each packet. Where did those numbers come from? How does every computer on Earth get its own address? And when you type a name like a website's address instead of a number, how does your computer find the right one? That is the mystery of the next part.

deepDive: Network engineers measure a connection's quality with two different numbers that are easy to mix up: bandwidth and latency. Bandwidth is how many bits per second a link can carry, like the width of a motorway. Latency is how long a single bit takes to make the trip, like the driving time. A fibre link across the Atlantic can have enormous bandwidth, yet its latency can never fall below the time light needs to cross the ocean in glass. Light in silica fibre travels at about 200,000 km/s because the glass has a refractive index of roughly 1.47, so the absolute minimum one-way delay is about 5 microseconds per kilometre. This is why some financial firms have paid for microwave radio links between trading centres: radio through air travels closer to the full speed of light, shaving off milliseconds. Packet size involves a trade-off too. Bigger packets waste less space on headers, but they hold a link longer and cost more to resend after an error; on a slow 14.4 kbit/s modem, one 1,500-byte packet tied up the line for about a second. The 1,500-byte Ethernet limit dates from early Ethernet designs and became so widespread that much of the Internet still assumes it, although data-centre networks often use 'jumbo frames' of around 9,000 bytes. If a packet is too big for a link, IPv4 routers can split it into fragments, but losing any fragment loses the whole packet, so modern systems prefer 'path MTU discovery', in which the sender learns the smallest limit along the route and sizes its packets to fit. Historians and engineers also debate how to describe the layers. The official OSI model of the 1980s has seven layers, while the Internet's own design documents describe four; the five-layer version taught in many classrooms is a blend. Finally, TCP's congestion control remains an active research area. The 1986 collapse led to Jacobson's algorithms, and newer schemes such as CUBIC and Google's BBR, plus the QUIC protocol that runs over UDP and now carries a large share of web traffic, keep refining how the Internet shares its roads fairly.
funFact: Every IPv4 packet carries a 'time to live' counter that each router lowers by one, so a packet that gets lost in a loop is thrown away instead of circling the Internet forever.

wrong: It switches the packet to a satellite
